prompt: Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: a production atlas of circular illustrated tokens for Creation, an original elemental myth about making a vast living world. The reference is the APPROVED STYLE AND CONTINUITY anchor, not a sheet to copy unchanged. Paint new subjects in exactly that family: luminous opaque gouache, selective fine ink contours, strong simplified silhouettes readable at 64px; deep lapis interiors, jade and turquoise, burnt ochre, muted coral, warm ivory light, very narrow ivory-gold rims. Not glossy coins or flat generic pictograms. Each icon is a complete perfect CIRCLE with opaque painted interior and transparent empty space outside. Center each circle in its own equal grid cell, circle diameter 80 percent of the shorter cell side, generous empty gutters. Absolutely no letters, names, numbers, grid lines, labels, UI, watermark or cast shadows outside circles. No modern laboratory hardware, books, houses or buildings. Only the specified object inside each circle, with a simple dark ground or essential local context. Tiny details must not carry the meaning. Related states should differ in structure, not merely colour. Follow item order exactly, left to right, top to bottom. Exactly 20 circles in 5 columns and 4 rows. Landscape atlas. Exact cell subjects: CELL 1, Tree dwellers: Two long-tailed primate-like mammals grip branching limbs with flexible hands and feet, one reaching toward a fruit while the other watches from above. Distinguish: Climbing furred vertebrates with grasping limbs, not insects, ground shrews or a warning-focused social scene. CELL 2, Whales: A large streamlined jade-grey whale curves through deep water beside a smaller calf, showing horizontal tail flukes, small foreflippers and a short exhalation at the surface. Distinguish: Mammal body, calf and horizontal flukes, without fish scales, gills or insect wings. CELL 3, Bats: One ochre-furred bat spreads broad dark-jade skin wings supported by long visible finger bones, with round ears, a small muzzle and two tiny hind feet. Distinguish: Fur and finger-supported membranes; no feathers, four separate insect wings or six legs. CELL 4, New food web: Young woodland holds a pollinating insect, fruiting sapling, small mammal and lean furred hunter, connected by a few curved ochre feeding paths that pass through seeds and soil. Distinguish: Reconnected post-impact woodland relationships, with the familiar broken trunk beneath; no sauropod giants or grassland-only chain. CELL 5, Recovering world: The same hook-marked planet now shows green young woodland spreading around a visible grey scar, with tiny mammal and insect silhouettes at the living edge and one stone track slab below. Distinguish: Renewed world still bears impact loss and fossil evidence; no living great browsers and no retreating ice front. CELL 6, Snowfall: Broad pale snow crystals and soft flakes fall from a cold jade-grey cloud onto the upper surface of a mountain glacier, accumulating as a fresh white cap. Distinguish: Falling flakes and new snow layer dominate, not rain streaks or an outward-moving thick ice front. CELL 7, Advancing ice: A thick blue-white ice front spreads outward from high mountains across an ochre valley, burying low ridges and pushing a dark moraine before its steep cracked edge. Distinguish: Outward expansion of sustained glacial ice, with no ash veil or receding green margin. CELL 8, River migration: A mixed line of small mammals and hoofed grazers follows a jade river downhill away from snowy peaks toward green lower country; the river remains the clear connecting route. Distinguish: Ground wildlife moves along a river corridor during climate change; no bird loop or one animal's remembered fruit route. CELL 9, Sheltered oasis: Several small mammals and a short-necked grazer gather beneath a dense green grove around a jade spring, protected by ochre rock while distant blue ice remains outside the warm enclosure. Distinguish: A reached climate refuge with varied travellers and distant ice, not an empty oasis or one hiding primate. CELL 10, Varied survivors: Four related pointed-nosed mammals stand together on neutral ground, sharing the same body plan but showing clearly thin, medium and thick fur coats already present in the group. Distinguish: Inherited coat differences coexist before selection; no single animal magically changing or universal white winter coats. CELL 11, Cold-adapted populations: Three thick-furred descendants of the same pointed-nosed small mammals forage beside snow and low sheltering rocks, including one smaller juvenile; all retain the ancestral ears and tail form. Distinguish: Reproducing population with thick coats in cold habitat, not an individual growing instant fur or a comparison of unselected coats. CELL 12, Surviving lineages: Two small family groups occupy adjoining habitats divided by a rock ridge: thin-furred mammals beside a green spring and thick-furred relatives beside lingering snow, each with a juvenile. Distinguish: Multiple enduring lineages and different routes through cold are shown together, without one universal winning animal. CELL 13, World after the ice: The recurring hook-marked planet has a retreating pale ice edge, jade rivers and green shoots spreading across exposed ochre land, with small mammals moving into the opening ground. Distinguish: Receding ice and recolonization are clear; preserve the same geography and exclude living great browsers. CELL 14, Attention: A close profile of the established long-tailed tree dweller leans toward a bright coral fruit, its wide dark eye and lifted grasping hand aligned with the object. Distinguish: Focused living gaze at a nearby target, not an isolated eye, recoiling danger response or human looking at stars. CELL 15, Fear: The same tree dweller crouches backward on a branch, gripping it tightly while a small lean predator silhouette appears below; the animal's eye is wide and tail drawn close. Distinguish: Visible defensive response to a perceived threat, rather than active hunting or a relaxed hidden animal. CELL 16, Safety: The tree dweller rests with a smaller companion inside a dense sheltered green grove, hidden behind interlocking branches while a distant predator passes outside the foliage. Distinguish: Concealment from a specific danger and relaxed posture, not a broad climate refuge or an alarm exchange. CELL 17, Memory: The tree dweller studies a familiar forked fruit branch; a faint second ivory outline of that same branch appears behind its head, while the real branch remains solid jade and coral. This double image is the recurring convention for remembered experience. Distinguish: One present object paired with a faint matching recollection, not a route, general gaze or sound passed between people. CELL 18, Learned path: A single tree dweller follows an ochre path around a dark ridge toward a fruiting tree partly hidden beyond it; a faint pale trace of the same route sits under its feet. Distinguish: One familiar route to a destination not visible from the starting point; no mass climate migration or seed carrying. CELL 19, Call: The tree dweller opens its mouth from a high branch, releasing three broad pale sound arcs into clear air while one companion remains partly hidden behind distant leaves. Distinguish: Single animal signal radiates outward without a returning wall reflection, human exchange or different bird motifs. CELL 20, Shared warning: One tree dweller calls from a branch while two companions turn sharply toward the same partly hidden predator; pale sound arcs link caller and listeners. Distinguish: Signal visibly changes several listeners' attention toward a threat; no solitary cry or calm group portrait. Keep the common circle size and painted finish. Anatomical lineages matter: insects have six legs, birds feathered wings, bats membranous finger-supported wings. A depicted early cell is a symbolic magnified view, not a modern laboratory slide. The world is not Earth's recognizable map. People, if listed, have varied warm earth-brown complexions, simplified features and no modern objects. Never add people, plants or animals to a subject that predates them. Do not draw the subject names.
